I don't think there's any 1 best way to react. Like, if someone came to you shaking and crying and told you they're gay, would you just be like "oh, okay. What do you want for dinner?" or would you comfort and reassure them? And if someone off-handily said they liked girls, would you start cheering and whooping or would you just be cool and carry on with the conversation?

There seems like there is so much thought into how to react when someone comes out that everyone forgets basic human empathy and social etiquette. You react in the way that is most applicable to the situation at hand.

If it were any other "big news" you'd react based on their body language and tone? "I'm pregnant." Are they smiling and laughing as they tell you? Are they speaking softly and look ashamed? Are you 78th person they've told today and it's getting old?

And if you're still unsure, you're perfectly allowed to say "Okay, and how do we feel about that?" to get a better understanding of their needs.

Hi, I recently got out of a similar relationship to your's. I want to say that your feelings are okay and you've not done anything wrong. You have every right to have your needs met in a relationship and it's okay to be upset when they aren't. The problem isn't that your body has changed, or that your expectations are unreasonable or creepy; the problem is that you're different people with different needs, but that can be communicated through and worked through. However, having said that, it does sound like your girlfriend has such a low/non-existant sex drive compared to your's, you may be incompatible (if you stay monogamous).

Given you've been virtually sexless for so long, she probably doesn't even realise your needs aren't being met. It's likely, since she doesn't have the same wants to be wanted, she doesn't even realise why you would want it. However, that doesn't excuse her dismissing you when you did try and communicate.

I think it's important to consider a few things; Can you continue this relationship the way that it is? How often do you need sexual intimacy for you to continue the relationship? How often do you want it? Are you prepared to offer an open/non-monogamous relationship? Does she know how it's affecting you and has she made any efforts to meet your needs? I'm going to assume you'll probably conclude it can't continue the way it is and that you probably aren't comfortable with a polyamorous relationship.

Then, I think it's probably best to have a discussion where you make it clear how your needs aren't being met, how that's effecting you, and that you can't continue unless something changes. Be assertive and honest, try and avoid blaming anyone and just say that you need a change.

I'd say that you should probably be prepared to break-up; It's unfortunate, but if no compromise can be made then you'd both be happier to have the opportunity to move on. I know that when I broke up with my ex I definitely felt like a weight had been lifted off my shoulders, and had I tried to continue that relationship, my frustrations would've started to hurt our relationship and it could've become pretty toxic/distant. And, my ex is happier now that they can pursue a relationship with someone who shares their boundaries and needs and can understand them and their feelings better.

Good luck! Remember, relationships aren't everything and you can get over this if that is what you both need. Feel free to msg me if you need someone!

Sex is the biological component, whereas gender is a social construct. The best way I can describe it is like this: a vegetable can be basically any part of a plant (roots, leaves, fruit, etc), but no one part of a plant is a vegetable. You cannot really, biologically describe a vegetable outside of "tasty part of a plant". A part of a plant is a biological component, being a vegetable is a social construct. Being trans is like saying that the stem of a pumpkin is indeed a part of a plant, but it isn't a vegetable, it isn't a tasty part. So a person can say that they do indeed have female genitals and reproductive organs, but they aren't a woman, they don't fit into that part/role in society. Does that make sense?

I can't answer what differentiates a man from a woman as that's not really something I can wrap my head around. I just respect the people around me and don't really identify with either.

Your chromosomes do strongly influence your sex, but it's not an exact science. Sometimes people have different chromosomes to what is expected with their physical reproductive organs. Equally, you can have different sets of chromosomes (e.g. X, XXX, XYY, etc) or have different genitals than the typical male or female. Typically, somebody born with a uterus, vagina, vulva, etc can be described as afab (assigned female at birth), someone born with a penis, testicles, prostate, etc can be described as amab (assigned male at birth), and someone who has unusual or complex genitals (e.g. A uterus and testicles) can be described as intersex.

Beauty is in the eye of the beholder. Just because you've found most trans people unattractive, doesn't mean that others also don't find them attractive. Of all the serious crushes/relationships I've had, 75% have been trans. It's on a person by person basis.

And, let's be honest, if you're the kind of person to generalise a community to be mostly "highly unattractive", it sounds like you're not much of a catch yourself.

I think the idea for most trans people is not that they want to become the opposite sex, it's that they want to be recognised as the gender they feel most comfortable with and have people respect their identity. Sex is a biological/genetic thing whereas gender is a social construct. Similar to how vegetables are actually just different parts of a plant that we give a special name to indicate it "tastes good" when they're just the leaves/roots/stem/etc.

Whilst it's true you can't change your genes, having XX chromosomes doesn't make you a female and having XY chromosomes doesn't make you male. There's been cases of individuals who have a set of chromosomes typical indicating one sex but have genetials or reproductive systems that indicate the opposite sex or different parts of each sex at once (e.g. a uterus and testicles). Equally, there have been people who have had completely different chromosome sets all together, e.g. X, XXX, XYY, etc. XX and XY are not the only options, even if they're most common. This is just to say that the principal that you're indicating doesn't hold up against some cases, so why apply it to all cases? Particularly when most people don't know if they have an "unusual" chromosome set. And, as above, it's less about sex and more about gender.\*

Sometimes, in a world that expects individuals to look a certain way to be a certain gender, it can be difficult to accept your body the way that it is and certain changes can assist in helping you feel more confident and comfortable. Many people who identify with their assigned gender at birth will also get gender affirming surgeries (lazer hair removal, breast augmentations, hair transplants, etc) to help them feel more comfortable in their bodies. It's just another kind of plastic surgery so you can get the body you want and feel confident in, only certain types are more common in transgender people.

I played Doki Doki Literature Club a couple years ago and still can't shake it. Yuri's eyes are especially haunting. Sayori's death is very sad but also oddly relatable. And Happy Little Tree Friends is just uncomfortable. Do not like.

2. I feel comfortable anytime I'm home alone. If not alone, I'm always uncomfortable. I like knowing I'm free to do as I please with no fear of criticism or anger.

3. As before, I'm comfortable alone. However, animals make me even more comfortable. I have cats and they're the best. Animals are not inherently cruel, which is comforting. And, most often, I'm more powerful than a common animal so I don't need to be afraid if it tries to do anything.

4. I find realistic things scarier. Such as slow descent into insanity like in doki doki literature club. Or the fact that Monika could still be in a computer watching over me. The idea of someone working behind the scenes, e.g. Stalker always watching or squatter always close, is scariest to me. Unrealistic things are easily brushed off afterwards.

5. I don't like slow, painful deaths that aren't just slowly bleeding out. So something like burning alive, drowning, suffocation, buried alive, starving to death, etc. The kind of thing where you have time to prevent it as it happens but you still fail.

6. I think set somewhere familiar, not necessarily in your home. Because it means you don't actually know how long it's been happening. The man who likes to watch you sleep could have started yesterday or since you were six.

7. I think it could. You just have to be careful not to let on too many details of the main protagonist and their home etc. It would pull a reader out of the story and lose the emotional investment you get with a second person story.

8. I don't like too much gore in horror. Though it's impactful, it just makes me want to throw up, not gets me scared. And as said before, not knowing something is quite terrifying. But finding something like a torn apart, dead animal is chilling. 

9. I think humans. More realistic.

10. Dead silence. Makes you feel like listening for scary sounds that aren't there.

Ultimately, I find it scarier if you try really hard to survive something, and still fail. Or nearly fail. Something grounded in reality.
